implementation_notes: std::sync::Condvar is the condition variable: wait() atomically unlocks the guard and blocks, and its documentation notes the call is susceptible to spurious wake-ups, so the predicate must be checked after every return; wait_while (since 1.42) takes that predicate as a closure and performs the loop for you, returning the guard once the condition no longer holds - the closest std equivalent of the classic guarded method. Use it with a Mutex<T> that owns the state (the lock guard is the proof of exclusivity), reach for a channel when the guard is 'a message is available', and use an async primitive for tasks on a runtime.
pitfalls: Mutex poisoning: a panic in another thread makes lock()/wait_while return Err, so decide explicitly whether poisoning is fatal or recoverable instead of unwrapping blindly.
A Condvar panics if it is used with more than one mutex over its lifetime, so keep the (Mutex, Condvar) pair private to one guarded object.
notify_one with no waiter is lost - the predicate under the mutex is the only memory of the transition.

variants.name: tokio::sync::Notify (async tasks)
variants.implementation_notes: On an async runtime the same guard is a Notify: notified().await suspends the task until notify_one() is called, and tokio documents the permit model - a notify issued before the await is remembered and consumed by the next notified(), while several concurrent waiters need Notified::enable() before re-checking the predicate to avoid a wake-up being consumed by the wrong waiter. Use it for task-based handoff over a Mutex-protected deque, wrap the await in tokio::time::timeout for a bounded wait, and stay on std Condvar when the waiter is an OS thread.
pitfalls: With several concurrent waiters the predicate must be re-checked after enable(), or a permit can be consumed by a task that finds nothing and sleeps again.
A missed notification has no timer: a future that never resolves hangs silently, so deadline logic belongs around the await.
